topic: Fix onboarding before you scale acquisition
content:
Most early-stage teams pour money into acquisition while their onboarding quietly leaks the users they already paid for.

Last spring I worked with a founder whose onboarding was leaking value at every step. New accounts stalled on an empty dashboard, support tickets piled up, and the team blamed the ads. We rebuilt the first-run flow around one job the user came to do. Within six weeks churn dropped by a third and support tickets fell by half.

The lesson is not "redesign your onboarding". It is: measure where new users stop, before you spend another dollar bringing more of them in.

Start with three numbers: time to first value, the step where most sessions end, and how many tickets arrive in week one. If you cannot name them today, that is your next sprint.

topic: Why AI pilots stall in small companies
content:
A 2025 MIT Sloan study of 1,200 SMEs found that 73% of AI pilots never reach production, and the ones that do take an average of 14 months to pay back.

The reason is rarely the model. It is data that lives in five spreadsheets, a process nobody wrote down, and no owner once the consultant leaves.

Before you buy another AI tool, answer three questions. Which decision will this change? Where does the data for that decision live today? Who owns the result in ninety days?

If any answer is "not sure", the pilot will stall no matter which vendor you pick.

content:
Splitting a seed-stage product into microservices feels like engineering maturity. Usually it is a tax you pay before you have revenue to pay it with.

A monolith with clear module boundaries gives you most of what you want: separate ownership, testable seams, and the option to extract a service later when one part genuinely needs to scale on its own.

One client of ours went the other way and spent a quarter merging eleven services back into one codebase; their deploy time went from two days to twenty minutes and they shipped more in the next month than in the previous six.

Extract a service when you can name the load, the team, or the failure mode that demands it. Not before.

content:
بدهی فنی در استارتاپ‌های نوپا یک‌شبه ساخته نمی‌شود. هر میان‌بری که برای رسیدن به دموی بعدی می‌زنیم، قسطی است که بعداً با بهره پس می‌دهیم.

پارسال با بنیان‌گذار یک استارتاپ پرداخت کار کردم که تیمش هر هفته دو روز کامل را صرف رفع باگ‌های تکراری می‌کرد. سه ماه روی بازنویسی ماژول پرداخت تمرکز کردیم. زمان انتشار نسخه‌ی جدید از ده روز به دو روز رسید و ریزش مشتری‌ها ۳۰ درصد کم شد.

درس این تجربه ساده است: بدهی فنی را مثل بدهی مالی ثبت کنید. فهرستش را داشته باشید، برای هر قلم هزینه‌ی ماهانه‌اش را تخمین بزنید و در هر اسپرینت بخشی از ظرفیت تیم را به پرداختش بدهید.

اگر نمی‌دانید از کجا شروع کنید، از ماژولی شروع کنید که بیشترین باگ تکراری را دارد.

content:
Picture a six-person team that ships every Friday and still feels slow. Nobody is idle. Every standup sounds busy. Yet the roadmap slips a little more each month.

In a team like that, the bottleneck is rarely effort. It is usually one of three things: work waiting on a single person's review, priorities that change mid-sprint, or tasks too large to finish inside a week.

You can test each one without a consultant. Count how many tickets sit in review for more than two days. Count how often the sprint goal changed after Monday. Count how many tickets carried over from last sprint.

Whichever number is highest is where to start. Fix that one before you add process anywhere else.
